sentence: A reliever inhaler eases symptoms when they happen, while a preventer is taken every day to reduce airway inflammation.
note: Reliever acts when symptoms appear; preventer daily to reduce inflammation.

sentence: A reliever is used when symptoms appear, and a preventer is taken every day, even when a person feels well, to reduce airway inflammation, according to Asthma + Lung UK.
note: Restates body sentences, same sources.

sentence: NHS Inform says a person with asthma should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own and should always have a preventer inhaler.
note: Restates body sentences, same sources.

sentence: The NHS says to rinse the mouth with water or brush the teeth after each dose of a steroid inhaler to help prevent thrush; Asthma + Lung UK says a spacer can also reduce steroid side effects.
note: Restates body sentences, same sources.

sentence: The NHS and Asthma + Lung UK both link needing a reliever more often than usual with asthma that is not well controlled; Asthma + Lung UK advises speaking to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.
note: Restates body sentences, same sources.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says to call 999 if the reliever is not helping in an asthma attack, and to ask for an urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment after managing an attack alone.
note: Restates body sentences, same sources.

sentence: A reliever inhaler is used when symptoms appear.
note: Reliever inhalers act fast when symptoms appear.

sentence: Blue reliever inhalers contain salbutamol, a short-acting bronchodilator, which is a medicine that quickly opens the airways.
note: Blue relievers contain salbutamol, a SABA that can quickly open the airways.

sentence: A preventer inhaler is taken every day, even when a person feels well, and works over time to reduce airway inflammation.
note: Preventers taken daily, even when well, reduce inflammation and sensitivity of the airways over time.

sentence: The two do different jobs.
note: Plain restatement of the two descriptions above.

sentence: NHS Inform says a person with asthma should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own and should always have a preventer inhaler.
note: NHS Inform: 'You should never be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own. You should always have a preventer inhaler.'

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK adds that relying only on a reliever makes symptoms and asthma attacks more likely.
note: A+LUK: using only a reliever makes symptoms and attacks more likely (summary; blended).

sentence: Salbutamol is the usual blue reliever.
note: Blue reliever contains salbutamol.

sentence: A preventer such as beclometasone is an inhaled steroid.
note: NHS steroid inhalers page and beclometasone pages list beclometasone as a steroid inhaler.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says a GP or nurse should discuss switching from a blue-only reliever to an anti-inflammatory reliever, known as an AIR inhaler, which combines a reliever with a low-dose steroid.
note: A+LUK: GP or nurse should discuss switching from blue-only reliever to AIR inhaler; AIR combines reliever with low-dose steroid.

sentence: The NHS says steroid inhalers should not be stopped without medical advice.
note: NHS steroid inhalers page: prescription-only, do not stop without medical advice.

sentence: In COPD, the NHS says short-acting bronchodilator inhalers are usually the first treatment.
note: NHS COPD treatment: short-acting bronchodilators first.

sentence: A steroid inhaler may be suggested if breathlessness continues on a long-acting inhaler or flare-ups stay frequent, and it is usually combined with a long-acting medicine in one inhaler.
note: NHS COPD treatment: steroid inhaler may be suggested if still breathless on long-acting inhaler or frequent flare-ups; usually combined.

sentence: A spacer is a chamber used with a pressurised metered-dose inhaler, the kind that sprays out a puff of medicine.
note: Plain device description; spacer page covers pMDI use with spacers.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says using a spacer can also prevent side effects from steroid medicines in preventer or combination inhalers.
note: 'Using a spacer can also prevent side effects from steroid medicines in preventer or combination inhalers.'

sentence: It also says a tight seal around the mouthpiece helps make sure the full dose is received, and that a whistling sound from the spacer means the person is breathing in too fast.
note: Tight seal helps full dose; whistling sound means breathing in too fast.

sentence: The NHS says to rinse the mouth with water or brush the teeth after each dose of a beclometasone inhaler, to help prevent thrush.
note: NHS beclometasone side effects: rinse mouth with water or brush teeth after each dose to prevent thrush.

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK gives similar advice, saying to rinse the mouth with water and spit it out after using an inhaler that contains steroid, to reduce the chance of side effects.
note: A+LUK spacers page: if inhaler contains steroid, rinse mouth with water and spit out to reduce chance of side effects.

sentence: The NHS steroid inhaler page also advises using a spacer.
note: Search summary: NHS steroid inhaler page also advises using a spacer.

sentence: The rinsing advice applies to inhalers that contain steroid.
note: A+LUK: 'if you've used an inhaler that contains steroids'.

sentence: The NHS lists shakiness, a faster heartbeat and headaches as the typical side effects of salbutamol.
note: Shakiness, faster heartbeat, headaches.

sentence: It says serious side effects are rare.
note: NHS: serious side effects are rare.

sentence: Muscle pain or weakness, muscle cramps, or an irregular or more noticeable heartbeat can be a sign of low potassium levels, and the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away if these happen.
note: Call a doctor or 111 straight away for muscle pain or weakness, cramps, irregular or more noticeable heartbeat, a sign of low potassium.

sentence: For beclometasone, the NHS lists oral thrush and a dry or sore throat as common side effects, and its steroid inhaler page also lists a hoarse or croaky voice.
note: Thrush and dry/sore throat common; steroid inhaler page lists sore mouth/throat, hoarse or croaky voice, thrush.

sentence: If thrush develops, the NHS says a pharmacist can recommend an antifungal mouth gel, and the beclometasone inhaler is kept up while the gel is used.
note: Pharmacist can recommend antifungal mouth gel; keep using inhaler while using antifungal.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or struggling breathing, or skin, lips or tongue turning blue, grey or pale, and for chest pain after using more than the recommended dose.
note: 999 list: swelling of lips, mouth, throat, tongue; fast or struggling breathing; blue/grey/pale; chest pain after more than recommended dose.

sentence: If more than the recommended dose has been used and the heartbeat is fast or noticeable, the NHS says to contact NHS 111.
note: Contact 111 if more than recommended dose and fast or more noticeable heartbeat.

sentence: The NHS says needing a salbutamol inhaler more often than usual could be a sign that the condition is not well controlled.
note: NHS salbutamol page: using more than usual could be a sign condition not well controlled (the page gives a weekly count, omitted).

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says regularly needing a reliever inhaler points to asthma that is not under control, and advises speaking to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.
note: A+LUK: frequent reliever use signals poorly controlled asthma; speak to GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist (count omitted).

sentence: Asthma + Lung UK says an asthma attack is an emergency, and that 999 should be called for an ambulance if the reliever is not helping.
note: A+LUK asthma attacks page: call 999 if reliever not helping (puff counts omitted).

sentence: It says to call 999 if a person feels worse at any point, and to call 999 straight away if there is no reliever inhaler to hand.
note: Feel worse at any point: 999. No blue reliever: call 999 straight away.

sentence: It adds that even a person who feels able to get to A&E should call 999 for an ambulance, so they can be treated on the way to hospital, and that the call handler should be told it is an asthma attack.
note: Tell call handler it's an asthma attack; call 999 even if able to get to A&E so treated on the way.

sentence: After an attack treated with the reliever alone, Asthma + Lung UK advises asking for an urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment.
note: If treated attack yourself with reliever, ask for urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment.
